newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bosnian "Romeo and Juliet" musical opens in Vienna.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian "Romeo and Juliet" musical opens in Vienna.

text.p: "Shakespeare, Romeo and Julia in Sarajevo" -- a toe-tapping opera musical of the bard's famous love story set against a backdrop of war-ravaged Bosnia -- opens in Vienna on Thursday.
"It's a marriage of the American musical with Slavic seriousness and pathos," flamboyant Russian composer Sergei Dreznin, who co-wrote the show with Sarajevo author Miroslav Prstojevic, told Reuters.

"The show makes you laugh and it makes you cry. It has the incredible emotional depth that Russian culture is famous for," he added. The songs are all original Shakespeare text while the dialogue is mostly in German.
The show, set in Bosnia in 1993, is based on the tragic real life romance between a Moslem woman, Admira Ismic, and Bosko Brkic, a Serb man.

The two were gunned down while fleeing besieged Sareajevo to get married and their bodies were left uncollected on front lines for days in one of the most emotionally wrenching episodes of Bosnia's war.
But the musical is not confined to the grim facts.
"It is a play all about Romeos and Julias in the whole of ex-Yugoslavia, not just this one pair," said Croatian co-director Dunja Tot.
The cast sport Levi 501s, RayBans and leather jackets and flash Motorola mobile phones as status symbols.
"Over-the-top romance and cynicism are what characterise life in ex-Yugoslavia," says Vienna-based Dreznin. "You have to have the best gun, the best Motorola and so on."
The story is portrayed with a lot of black humour -- an essential component of life in Yugoslavia, Dreznin says.
The cast is multinational, with the two protagonists from Bosnia and the other actors from Croatia, Serbia, the United States and Austria.

The musical originally opened in Vienna in 1995 and then went on tour in Bosnia and Croatia, just two months after the Dayton peace accord was signed to end the bloody 43-month conflict in the region.
"In Vienna, audiences were really touched but in Bosnia they were less so because the reality was much worse," Tot said.
Although the Austrian capital is much more at home with the traditional cultural forms of concerts and opera, Dreznin was optimistic the show would also be a success the second time round.
"The problem of racial tolerance is a burning question in Austria, so the show is very topical," he said.
Dreznin first set Shakespeare to music in 1983 with his Hamlet adaptation "Ophelia: An Opera in Blue", which was performed in fringe theatres in Britain, Austria and Russia.
"For a Russian it was not difficult to put Shakespeare's words to music because it was not a holy cow for me. It worked perfectly with Pushkin too," he noted.
He sees himself as a pioneer in the musical field, inspired by George Gershwin and Andrew Lloyd Webber.
"People need something remarkable for the end of the millenium. This is exciting and modern, a unique experience relating to true feelings," he said.
